title: Weighted Uniform Strings
directAnswer: A uniform substring is a run of one repeated character; its weight is the character's alphabet position (a=1…z=26) times the run length. Precompute every achievable weight in a single left-to-right pass — keep a running sum that resets when the character changes and adds the char weight when it repeats — storing each running value in a hash set. Then answer each query in O(1) by membership test. O(n + q) time, O(n) space.

rules: Weight of a uniform substring = `charWeight × runLength`, where `w(a)=1 … w(z)=26`.
Only **contiguous runs of the same character** are uniform — `"ab"` is never uniform.
Accumulate within a run (`running += w(c)`) and **reset** to `w(c)` when the character changes.
Store every intermediate running value — each prefix of a run is itself a valid uniform substring.
Precompute the set **once**, then every query is an O(1) membership check.

You can enumerate all achievable values cheaply and cache them

remember.takeaway: When a problem fires many membership queries against a derivable set of values, precompute the whole set once and answer each query in O(1). Here the set is every prefix-weight of every same-character run, built in one pass with a resettable running sum.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you separate one-time preprocessing from per-query work, and whether you correctly enumerate every prefix of each run (not just the full run) into the lookup set.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Only inserting the full run's weight (missing shorter prefixes), or recomputing weights per query for an O(n·q) blow-up.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Frame it as 'precompute the achievable-weight set in O(n), then O(1) per query', and note each step of the running sum already represents a valid uniform-substring weight, so insertion is free.

problemStatement:
The **weight** of a character is its 1-based position in the alphabet: `a = 1, b = 2, …, z = 26`. A **uniform** string is one made of a single repeated character (e.g. `"ccc"`). The **weight of a uniform string** is the character weight times its length (e.g. `"ccc" = 3 × 3 = 9`).

Given a string `s` and a list of integer `queries`, for each query determine whether there exists a **uniform substring** of `s` whose weight equals the query. Output `"Yes"` or `"No"` for each query.
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters
understanding: Uniform substrings live entirely inside maximal runs of one character. Within a run of character c of length L, the achievable weights are w(c)·1, w(c)·2, …, w(c)·L — exactly the running totals as you extend the run one character at a time. So a single pass that accumulates within a run and resets on a character change visits every achievable weight. Cache them; queries become set lookups.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Does a uniform substring have to be a full run, or can it be a prefix of a run?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Any contiguous block of identical characters counts — so every prefix length of a run is valid. That's why we store each intermediate running sum.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How is weight defined exactly?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: character weight (a=1…z=26) multiplied by the number of repeats. "aaa" = 3, "bb" = 4, "d" = 4.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How many queries should I expect?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Potentially up to 10⁵, so per-query work must be O(1) — precompute the answer set first.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can two different runs produce the same weight?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — "bb" (4) and "d" (4) both weigh 4. A set naturally deduplicates; we only care about achievability.

examples.explanation: Achievable weights: a→1; b→2; c→3,6; d→4,8,12; e→5. Set = {1,2,3,4,5,6,8,12}. 1,3,12,5 present; 9,10 absent.
Run of 'a' length 3 → weights 1, 2, 3. 4 is unreachable.
Runs are 'a'(1), 'b'(2), 'a'(1) → achievable set {1, 2}. The lone 'b' weighs 2 → Yes; nothing weighs 4 → No.

Doing that independently for each of q queries rescans the whole string q times — O(n·q).
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each query triggers a full O(n) scan of the runs; with q queries that's O(n·q). Only O(1) extra space since nothing is cached.
approaches.explanation:
Answer each query in isolation: walk the runs of `s`, maintaining a running weight, and report `"Yes"` the moment a running value equals the query (else `"No"`).

**Why it's correct.** It directly checks the achievability condition for the one query in hand.

**Why we improve it.** The set of achievable weights does not change between queries, yet this recomputes it from scratch every time. With up to 10⁵ queries over a 10⁵ string that's 10¹⁰ operations — far too slow. The fix is to compute the achievable set once and reuse it.
approaches.insight: Repeated identical scans are a flashing sign to precompute. The achievable-weight set is query-independent, so building it a single time and caching converts O(n·q) into O(n + q).

dryRun.intro: Rescan the single 'a' run for each query.

code.python:
def weighted_uniform_strings(self, s: str, queries: list[int]) -> list[str]:
    res = []
    for q in queries:
        found = False
        running = 0
        prev = ''
        for c in s:
            running = running + (ord(c) - 96) if c == prev else (ord(c) - 96)
            prev = c
            if running == q:
                found = True
                break
        res.append('Yes' if found else 'No')
    return res

approaches.name: Precompute Achievable-Weight Set (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The intended answer — one pass builds a hash set of every achievable weight, then O(1) per query.
hints: The achievable weights don't depend on the queries. What if you computed them all once?
Scan s once; keep a running sum that adds w(c) when the char repeats and resets to w(c) otherwise. Insert every running value into a set.
Each query is then just a set membership test → O(1).
approaches.complexityReasoning: Building the set is one O(n) pass with O(1) work per character. Each of the q queries is an O(1) set lookup → O(n + q) total. The set holds at most n distinct values → O(n) space.
approaches.explanation:
Make one left-to-right pass. Track `running` (the weight of the current run prefix) and `prev` (the previous character). For each character `c`: if `c == prev`, extend the run with `running += w(c)`; otherwise start a new run with `running = w(c)`. After updating, insert `running` into a hash set. Once the pass is done, answer each query with a single membership check.

**Why each intermediate value matters.** Inside a run of `c` of length `L`, the prefixes have weights `w(c)·1, w(c)·2, …, w(c)·L`. The running sum hits each of those in turn, so inserting it at every step records every achievable uniform-substring weight — not just the full run. Inserting only the final `running` would miss the shorter prefixes and produce wrong `"No"`s.

**Why the reset is essential.** When the character changes, the previous run ends; the new run's weights start fresh from `w(c)`. Failing to reset would chain unrelated runs together and fabricate weights that no uniform substring actually has.

**Why a set.** Different runs can yield identical weights (`"bb"` and `"d"` both weigh 4). We only care whether a weight is achievable, so a set deduplicates naturally and gives O(1) lookups.

**Why this is the right complexity split.** Preprocessing is paid once (O(n)); each query is O(1). That's the canonical 'build an index, then serve fast lookups' trade, ideal when queries are numerous.
approaches.insight: The achievable-weight set is a tiny precomputed index over the string. Whenever queries are independent of each other and depend only on a fixed structure, compute that structure once and serve queries in O(1) — the same idea behind prefix sums and hashed lookups.

dryRun.intro: Build the set in one pass; resets shown where the character changes.

code.python:
def weighted_uniform_strings(self, s: str, queries: list[int]) -> list[str]:
    seen = set()
    running = 0
    prev = ''
    for c in s:
        w = ord(c) - 96
        running = running + w if c == prev else w
        seen.add(running)
        prev = c
    return ['Yes' if q in seen else 'No' for q in queries]

Every prefix weight of the run is itself achievable — record it.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Missing prefix weights
commonMistakesDetailed.why: A uniform substring can be any prefix of a run, so "ddd" yields 4, 8, AND 12. Inserting only the final 12 makes queries for 4 or 8 wrongly answer No.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
# only the full run
run_len = ...
seen.add(w * run_len)
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
running = running + w if c == prev else w
seen.add(running)  # every step

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Not resetting across runs
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Without the reset, the running sum carries over from a previous character, producing weights that no single-character substring actually has.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Per-query rescanning
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The achievable set is query-independent. Recomputing it for each query turns O(n + q) into O(n·q), which TLEs at 10⁵ queries.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
for q in queries:
    ...scan whole string...
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
# build seen once
return ['Yes' if q in seen else 'No' for q in queries]
